source.title: Dynamic Reflections: Probing Video Representations with Text Alignment
source.authors: Tyler Zhu; Tengda Han; Leonidas Guibas; Viorica Pătrăucean; Maks Ovsjanikov

record.tranche_reason: Applies the mutual k-NN alignment measure used in the cited original work to video-text pairs and reports results across models and test-time settings.
record.gate_note: The study reports alignment scores, their relationship to downstream performance, changes with the number of frames and captions, and temporal/cross-model alignment results. It also cites prior alignment findings, which are not recorded as results here. Figure 2 retrieval-performance correlations and Figure 4 downstream-task correlations are included because they report how alignment relates to model performance.
record.test_reason: Uses the original mutual k-NN metric with best-layer selection to measure vision–text alignment. It applies it to video–caption pairs across about 85 vision and 30 language encoders, and relates alignment to model capability (retrieval, downstream tasks). This is the same method and measure as the PRH cross-modal analysis, in a new (video) setting. It also varies test-time inputs and k, and measures video–video alignment.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that video–text alignment is an informative zero-shot probe that correlates with downstream performance on semantic and non-semantic tasks (point tracking excepted). Alignment roughly doubles with richer test-time inputs (more frames, more captions), which a saturation scaling law captures (R²>0.98). They argue the low alignment in prior work is largely due to impoverished test data. They also note native video models use frames better than image models, yet many video models are beaten by frame-averaged image models. Generative video models align weakly with text.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the mutual k-NN alignment metric and layer-pair selection approach, extending the input setting to video frames and multiple captions; it also introduces test-time scaling analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment changes with the number of frames, number and diversity of captions, and k setting. The paper also reports differences across vision and text encoders and across downstream tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Video–text alignment drops only slightly against temporally reordered negative captions; more aligned models drop more. LLM features rank captions in a bag-of-words fashion on Test of Time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal alignment measured by mutual k-NN is largely insensitive to temporal order, especially on the text side.

record.problems: Most scaling and temporal-alignment point values are presented in figures rather than described numerically in text. Correlation with capability is not a controlled model-size sweep and does not establish causal effects of size or training. Some downstream-task correlation reporting is internally hard to reconcile: the text calls point tracking weak, while Figure 4 gives R = 0.820, p = 0.007.

untested.parts: No controlled model-size or data sweep; independently trained models of different objectives are not compared within modality apart from the qualitative video–video clustering.
Does not vary language-model capability systematically with the vision side; most analyses fix Gemma2-9B-it.
Not tested; no mapping or stitching.
No comparison of different similarity metrics (only mutual k-NN); no out-of-distribution tests.
Whether shared data or objectives cause the alignment is not tested; only qualitative clustering by objective is shown.

missing.what: Saturation-fit S∞ and R² for other models and for PVD (e.g. pe_core_giant 0.405/0.417, videoprism 0.400, pe_core_large 0.109, vivit 0.209)
Full alignment matrices for about 85 vision × 30 language encoders, single caption and all ten captions; best results exceed those of Huh et al.
With ten captions, image models (even on a single frame) outperform many video models; the ranking of models changes with test-time input
Video generative models' alignment with text is described as quite weak (no numbers given)
Video vs image average alignment difference of +0.014; image-only models capped below 0.22

record.verdict_notes: V2 links were removed from the test-time input rows: they measure input dependence, not capability. The Figure 4 labels appear scrambled in the extracted text, and the prose suggests R=0.396 is point tracking and R=0.820 is Kinetics. Correlations are across heterogeneous models; there is no controlled scale sweep. Best-layer selection maximizes alignment, which may inflate scores.

versions.untested_parts: Does not isolate model size, training data, architecture, or objective while holding other factors fixed; it does not establish a general scaling trend across independently trained models.
Does not test whether increasing the capability of both the vision and language model together raises alignment; most reported comparisons use a fixed text encoder.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired-space interchangeability test.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified.
Tests changes in test-time inputs and the k setting, but does not compare different similarity metrics or report out-of-distribution tests.
Reports incomplete alignment and model clusters, but does not establish that shared training data or objectives cause the alignment, nor compare those causes against a common-world explanation.
